title: Sampling Distributions for Sample Means
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 4.1 Sampling Distributions for Sample Means
intro: Describe the center, spread, and shape of sample-mean distributions and calculate probabilities about averages.

moments.title: What varies
moments.text: The distribution describes sample means over repeated samples of a fixed size.

moments.title: Unbiased means
moments.text: The center of the sampling distribution equals the population mean.

moments.title: Spread of sample means
moments.text: Independent observations give a sampling SD equal to the population SD divided by the square root of sample size.

moments.title: Larger samples
moments.text: Larger samples produce less variable sample means.

moments.title: Normal populations
moments.text: Means from a normal population have a normal distribution at any sample size.

moments.title: Central limit theorem
moments.text: Large samples can make sample means approximately normal, even for a nonnormal population.

moments.title: University study times
moments.text: Keep the population SD separate from the SD of sample means.

moments.title: Probability for an average
moments.text: Standardize using the sampling SD, not the population SD.

moments.title: A percentile of sample means
moments.text: Find a cutoff on the distribution of sample means.

cards.name: Randomness and independence
cards.text: Use a random sample. For sampling without replacement, check the sample is no more than 10% of the population.

cards.name: Center and spread
cards.text: $\mu_{\bar x}=\mu$ and $\sigma_{\bar x}=\sigma/\sqrt n$ for independent observations.

cards.name: Shape
cards.text: A normal population gives normal means; for nonnormal populations, large samples support an approximation. Extreme skewness may require much more than 30.

cards.name: What is the event?
cards.text: A statement about an average concerns the sample-mean distribution, not an individual observation.

questions.obj: Find a probability for a sample mean
questions.q: The video models university study times as normal with mean 42 minutes and SD 8 minutes. For a random sample of nine students, find the probability the sample mean exceeds 45 minutes. Assume at least 90 students in the population.

work.text: The population is normal, the sample is random, and the stated population size supports the 10% condition.
The event concerns a mean from nine students.

questions.answer: About 13.03% of random samples of nine students would have a mean study time above 45 minutes.

questions.obj: Find an upper percentile for sample means
questions.q: For the same university model and sample size nine, find the cutoff for the top 1% of sample means.

work.text: The upper 1% starts at cumulative probability 0.99.
Use the mean 42 and sampling SD 8 divided by 3.
The cutoff describes averages of nine study times, not individual study times.

questions.answer: About 1% of sample means exceed 48.204 minutes.

steps.title: Create the sampling distribution
steps.suppose: we want a model for mean study time from nine students.
steps.observe: Use the sampling standard deviation, not 8. For nine students, the square root of the sample size is 3, so the exact sampling SD is 8/3.

steps.title: Find an upper-tail probability
steps.suppose: we want the probability that the mean exceeds 45 minutes.
do: On the distribution item, open [[Cumulative Probability]].
steps.observe: The shaded right tail describes averages of nine students, rather than individual study times.

steps.title: Find the upper one-percent cutoff
steps.suppose: we want the sample mean that starts the highest 1%.
do: On the same distribution, open [[Cumulative Probability]] if necessary.
steps.observe: The reported bound leaves 1% of sample means above it. The equivalent cumulative probability is 0.99.

traps.title: SD of individuals versus averages
traps.better: For nine independent students, $\sigma_{\bar x}=8/\sqrt9$ minutes.

traps.title: The population changes shape
traps.weak: The CLT makes the population normal.
traps.better: The CLT describes the sampling distribution of a mean; it does not change the population.

traps.title: A universal sample-size rule
traps.weak: Thirty observations guarantee a normal approximation.
traps.better: Extreme skewness or influential observations may require a substantially larger sample.

traps.title: What a probability refers to
traps.weak: 13% of individuals study more than 45 minutes.
traps.better: This calculation concerns averages of nine students, not individual students.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The CLT supplies an approximation, not a guarantee at a particular sample size. The university example explicitly assumes at least 90 students to justify sampling independence.

questions.stem: A population has mean 80 and SD 12. For independent samples of size 36, what are the mean and SD of the sample mean?
why: The mean stays 80 and the SD is 12/6=2.
Dividing by n rather than its square root is incorrect.
Center and spread have been reversed.

questions.stem: Which change halves the SD of a sample mean?
why: The SD is divided by the square root of 2.
The square root of the sample size doubles.
An additive change has no fixed proportional effect.

questions.stem: A population is normal. Independent random samples of size 8 are drawn. The sample-mean distribution is:
opts: Not normal because n is below 30
why: Normality of the population suffices here.
Its SD is reduced by the square root of 8.
The 30 guideline is unnecessary for a normal population.

questions.stem: What does a 0.04 probability that a sample mean exceeds 90 describe?
opts: 4% of repeated samples of the specified size have means above 90
why: Individuals are not the sampling units of this distribution.
An event probability is not a mean.
This probability is not a sampling fraction.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: Parcel masses are normally distributed with mean 500 g and SD 40 g. A random sample of 25 is selected without replacement from 10,000 parcels.
parts: (a) Describe the sampling distribution of the mean and justify conditions.
(b) Calculate the probability the sample mean exceeds 516 g.
(c) Describe the effect of increasing the sample size to 100.
sample: (a) The sample is random and 25 is no more than 10% of 10,000. The population is normal, so the sample mean is normal with mean 500 g and SD 40/√25=8 g.
(b) The standardized boundary is (516−500)/8=2, so the probability is about 0.0228.
(c) The center remains 500 g and the sampling SD becomes 40/√100=4 g. Means become less variable, while the population distribution stays the same.
checklist: Checks randomness and the sampling fraction.
Gives mean 500 and sampling SD 8 g.
Standardizes correctly and finds the upper tail.
Explains unchanged center and reduced sampling variability.
